--- title: "1.4 Importing, exploring, and exporting data" ---
![](../../src/images/hex_complex.png){.intro_image} In this lesson, we will cover the basics of interacting with files stored on your hard drive. While the content herein is very introductory, there are many elements that advanced users will find useful. Across this lesson, you will learn: - Formatting considerations for R scripts and code - Why you should always work in a project - How to read data from different file types (*this section includes a fairly long video and written review of the video content*) - Data exploration steps you should take whenever you read in a file - How to write different kinds of files to your hard drive (and why you should do so sparingly) *Note: Don't worry about my mention of creating a project in the video -- the project in `r_skills_data.zip` is already set up for you.* *Note: Create a new script file for this lesson and save it as `scripts/1.4_importing_exploring_exporting.R`.* ::: {.callout-important} This lesson assumes that you have completed the preliminary lessons. As the material covered herein will build on the content in those lessons, please do not proceed until their completion. :::
## Data for this lesson We will use the following real datasets in this lesson: **Global populations and CO~2~ emissions: API_EN.ATM.CO2E...csv**: These data were compiled by the [World Bank DataBank](https://databank.worldbank.org/home.aspx) and provide information on the emissions of greenhouse gases and the populations of countries around the world. Neither the tabular data nor the name of the file were modified from the original version. **Iris: iris.csv and iris.rds**: This is Edgar Anderson's famous data set that provides the measurements of flowers of three species of iris, *Iris setosa*, *I. versicolor*, and *I. virginica*. See `?iris` for more information (or the original paper at [this link](https://www.jstor.org/stable/2394164)!). **My Covid garden: my_covid_garden.rds, my_covid_garden.csv, and my_covid_garden.xlsx**: This is a tabular data set (in different formats) that describes a pretty unsuccessful raised bed garden at my home in Takoma Park, Maryland. **Portal rodents: portal.csv and portal.xlsx**: These data sets provide measurements taken in a long-term study (the Portal project) on rodent traits in Portal, Arizona. The provided data were collected in a fixed grid established in 1977 and include when an individual was measured, where the measurement occurred, the sex and species of the individual, and their hindfoot length. You can read more about this study and the data they collected at [this link](https://portal.weecology.org/). I intentionally made the data a good bit messier than the original version. ## Reading data Reading data imports data from a file or remote source into the current R session. Please watch and code along with the video below. I review some key concepts that I hope you gathered from our previous lessons and break new ground with a description of the process of reading data into R. {{< video https://www.youtube.com/embed/S9sySXd3VYc?si=Fc1FACb57ceIHxXQ >}} ### Review: Why work in a project? We will do all of our reading, exploring, and writing data from inside of an RStudio project. Projects have many benefits -- probably the largest of them is that all paths to data and code are supplied relative to your project folder. For example, I am working in a project called `r_skills`. The path to my `r_skills` folder (the working directory of my project) is: ``` /Users/brianevans/r_skills ``` This project contains a subfolder called `data` and in that folder is a subfolder called `raw`. The full path to the folder `raw` is therefore: ``` /Users/brianevans/r_skills/data/raw ``` The `raw` data folder contains a *.csv* file called `portal.csv`. The full path to this file is: ``` /Users/brianevans/r_skills/data/raw/portal.csv ``` Reading data with a full file path is super cumbersome (**Do not run!**): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_csv("/Users/brianevans/r_skills/data/raw/my_covid_garden.csv") ``` ::: The above has two problems: - If we share our code with others or change our folder structure, the file path will need to be modified - That is a lot of writing for each file that we read in! When we work within a project, the folder that contains the *.Rproj* file is the working directory for the project. The path to our files within the working directory is written as a **relative file path**. A relative file path is the path to a file *relative* to the working directory. Given that my working directory is the folder `r_skills`, the reading operation above would be written as: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_csv("data/raw/my_covid_garden.csv") ``` ::: In Base R, we can set our working directory using the function `setwd()`. Before RStudio came along, this function was at the top of most of our scripts. It might have looked something like this (**Do not run!**): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # My code for the tutorial: reading, exploring, and writing data # setup -------------------------------------------------------- library(tidyverse) # Set working directory: setwd("/Users/brianevans/r_skills") # Read in data: read_csv("data/raw/my_covid_garden.csv") ``` ::: This certainly helps reduce the amount of writing required to read in files. However ... ::: mysecret   [Avoid using `setwd()`!]{style="font-size: 20px"} Using `setwd()` in your code is less portable than sharing code managed in RStudio projects. Doing so requires you to communicate to others (and your future self) to modify their working directory to match the location on their file systems. When you share a **project** with your collaborators, everything will already be in place for them to execute the code. Even more importantly, you might change your mind about where you want to put your code or files. If you move your files to a new location, your code will no longer run until you modify the path within the `setwd()` function. Your code will be "broken" until you repair file paths. When you use projects, you can move your project anywhere you want in your file system and R will still be able to find your files. ::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} You are working inside your project. Which path should you use to read `my_covid_garden.csv`?
::: ### Review: Read csv files Tabular data are most often stored as a **CSV file** -- "CSV" stands for "comma-separated values." Data in this format are stored as plain-text files in which commas separate values, and each record (e.g., row in a data frame) is placed on a new line. A csv file is a comparatively simple, open, plain-text format that can be used widely across computer programs. It is best to read in *.csv* files with the *readr* function `read_csv()` (*Note: Remember that the readr package is a part of the core tidyverse!*). If we are working in a project, we supply the relative file path inside of parentheses. Let's read in the file `my_covid_garden.csv` from the folder `data/raw` and assign the object to the name `my_garden`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_garden <- read_csv("data/raw/my_covid_garden.csv") ``` ::: Notice that the above printed information about how R read in the data (i.e., conversion of raw data to a tibble). You should always read this information, as it may provide clues to potential problems! When tabular data are read in using `read_csv()`, the data are arranged into a tibble data frame: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_garden ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: Conversely, when data are read in using the base R function `read.csv()`, no additional information is printed and the data are arranged into a standard data frame (*Note: I have chosen to save space by hiding the output from the below, but please run this on your own!*): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_garden_df <- read.csv("data/raw/my_covid_garden.csv") ``` ::: ::: mysecret    [Do not use `read.csv()`!]{style="font-size: 20px"} Whenever you use `read.csv()`, additional exploration steps are necessary to search for errors in your data (see Data exploration, below). It is best to avoid this function. While you should take a moment to validate and explore almost every data file when you read it for the first time, `read_csv()` saves you a couple of steps in the process! ::: #### Sometimes reading a csv file is not as easy as it should be ... While encoding is not a problem with *.csv* files, there are often issues with the data that mess up the reading process. For example, the table below represents raw data that I obtained from the World Bank website: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_csv("data/raw/API_EN.ATM.CO2E.PC_DS2_en_csv_v2_2764620.csv") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 268 × 3 `Data Source` `World Development Indicators` ...3 1 Last Updated Date 2021-07-30 2 Country Name Country Code "Indicator Name,I… 3 Aruba ABW "CO2 emissions (m… 4 Africa Eastern and Southern AFE "CO2 emissions (m… 5 Afghanistan AFG "CO2 emissions (m… 6 Africa Western and Central AFW "CO2 emissions (m… 7 Angola AGO "CO2 emissions (m… 8 Albania ALB "CO2 emissions (m… 9 Andorra AND "CO2 emissions (m… 10 Arab World ARB "CO2 emissions (m… # ℹ 258 more rows ``` ::: ::: Here, we can see that a weird column name was added to the data -- a missing column name was replaced with the unhelpful column name `...3`. Looking at the data in the tibble above, we can see the source of the problem. It seems that the character values associated with *what should have been the column names* were printed on the second row of the data frame. This suggests that the top rows of the tabular data contained information that should not be a part of the data frame. Additional arguments can be passed to `read_csv()` to address this problem (and others; see `?read_csv`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_csv( "data/raw/API_EN.ATM.CO2E.PC_DS2_en_csv_v2_2764620.csv", skip = 4, skip_empty_rows = FALSE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 266 × 66 `Country Name` `Country Code` `Indicator Name` `Indicator Code` `1960` 1 Aruba ABW CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 205. 2 Africa Eastern and… AFE CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 0.906 3 Afghanistan AFG CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 0.0461 4 Africa Western and… AFW CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 0.0909 5 Angola AGO CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 0.101 6 Albania ALB CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 1.26 7 Andorra AND CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC NA 8 Arab World ARB CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 0.609 9 United Arab Emirat… ARE CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 0.119 10 Argentina ARG CO2 emissions (… EN.ATM.CO2E.PC 2.38 # ℹ 256 more rows # ℹ 61 more variables: `1961` , `1962` , `1963` , `1964` , # `1965` , `1966` , `1967` , `1968` , `1969` , # `1970` , `1971` , `1972` , `1973` , `1974` , # `1975` , `1976` , `1977` , `1978` , `1979` , # `1980` , `1981` , `1982` , `1983` , `1984` , # `1985` , `1986` , `1987` , `1988` , `1989` , … ``` ::: ::: ::: mysecret    [Read the help files!]{style="font-size: 20px"} Whenever you use a function for the first time, or use a function to address a new application, it is a best practice to read the help file for that function (e.g., `?read_lines`). Because functions may change over time, it is also worthwhile to revisit their help files on occasion. ::: ### Review: Read RDS files **RDS files** are the most straightforward file type to read in (but see the caveat associated with these files in "Writing data", below). RDS files are data sets that are written in, and written for, R. We can read in an RDS file with the function `read_rds()`. Let's read in the file `my_covid_garden.rds`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_rds("data/raw/my_covid_garden.rds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: Notice that the first column, `bed`, is an integer and `light_access` and `species` were read in as factors. When you read in an RDS file, the returned object contains all of the classes and attributes of the object when it was written. ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} What is a key advantage of using an RDS file for an object that will remain in R?
::: ### Review: Read Excel files Excel files can be challenging to read into R but luckily the package `readxl` has made the process fairly straightforward (*Note: readxl is a tidyverse package, but not a member of the core tidyverse*). Each table in an Excel file is typically stored within worksheets (the tabs on the bottom of the Excel window). Before we read in an Excel file, we should check how many worksheets are present. To do so, we use the function `readxl::excel_sheets()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} readxl::excel_sheets("data/raw/my_covid_garden.xlsx") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "my_beds" "garden_life" ``` ::: ::: The above returned an atomic character vector with two values, where each value represents the name of a worksheet in the file `my_covid_garden.xlsx`. By default, the function `readxl::read_excel()` will read in *only* the first worksheet in the file (and return a tibble data frame): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} readxl::read_excel("data/raw/my_covid_garden.xlsx") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 26 × 2 species bed 1 lion's mane 0 2 oyster mushrooms 0 3 shitake 0 4 oyster mushrooms 0 5 shitake 0 6 shitake 0 7 oyster mushrooms 0 8 lion's mane 0 9 lion's mane 0 10 jalapenos 1 # ℹ 16 more rows ``` ::: ::: If we would like to read in a different worksheet, we can supply the argument `sheet = [name of sheet]` (Note: See `?readxl::read_excel`): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} readxl::read_excel( "data/raw/my_covid_garden.xlsx", sheet = "garden_life" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 47 × 5 `Here is what happened in my covid garden!` ...2 ...3 ...4 ...5 1 2 bed light_access species date event 3 1 full sun NA 43766 appl… 4 2 full sun NA 43767 appl… 5 3 full sun NA 43770 appl… 6 4 full sun NA 43774 appl… 7 5 full sun NA 43777 appl… 8 6 full sun NA 43777 appl… 9 0 deep shade NA 43875 cut … 10 0 deep shade lion's … 43882 plug… # ℹ 37 more rows ``` ::: ::: In the above, we notice that there are quite a few bad column names and that what are most likely the correct column names are printed on the second line of data. We can add a `skip = [number of rows]` argument to skip the first two rows of data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} readxl::read_excel( "data/raw/my_covid_garden.xlsx", sheet = "garden_life", skip = 2 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun NA 2019-10-28 00:00:00 applied compost 2 2 full sun NA 2019-10-29 00:00:00 applied compost 3 3 full sun NA 2019-11-01 00:00:00 applied compost 4 4 full sun NA 2019-11-05 00:00:00 applied compost 5 5 full sun NA 2019-11-08 00:00:00 applied compost 6 6 full sun NA 2019-11-08 00:00:00 applied compost 7 0 deep shade NA 2020-02-14 00:00:00 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 00:00:00 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 00:00:00 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 00:00:00 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}}  [When working with the lesson data, please avoid opening an .xlsx file with Excel!]{style="font-size: 20px"} I recommend avoiding the temptation to peek at an Excel file in Microsoft Excel. That is because, if a file is saved, Excel can alter the values (e.g., change the encoding associated with a variable). When working with dates, this can lead to huge issues! ::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} Reorder the lines below to read the `garden_life` worksheet and skip its first two rows. One line uses the wrong function. Leave it in the trash.

::: ## Data exploration Whenever we read in data, it is crucial to take the time to explore its class, structure, composition, and the distribution of values. ### Data structure If we read in a non-tibble data frame, we should be sure to explore the structure with `str()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} str(my_garden_df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 45 obs. of 5 variables: $ bed : int 1 2 3 4 5 6 0 0 0 0 ... $ light_access: chr "full sun" "full sun" "full sun" "full sun" ... $ species : chr NA NA NA NA ... $ date : chr "2019-10-28" "2019-10-29" "2019-11-01" "2019-11-05" ... $ event : chr "applied compost" "applied compost" "applied compost" "applied compost" ... ``` ::: ::: In the above, we see the number of observations (rows) and number of variables (columns). We are also given information on the name and class of each column and the first few values in each. In a tibble data frame, structural information is printed by default: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_garden ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: Despite this handy printing of the tibble, we often need to use the number of rows or columns in a data frame programmatically. We can determine the number of rows with `nrow()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(my_garden) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 45 ``` ::: ::: ... and determine the number of columns with `ncol()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ncol(my_garden) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: We can return the number of rows and columns at the same time using the function `dim()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dim(my_garden) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 45 5 ``` ::: ::: This returned the number of rows (the first number) and columns (the second number) as an integer vector. ::: mysecret {{< fa screwdriver-wrench size=2x >}} [What is the *length* of a data frame?]{style="font-size: 1.25em; padding-left: 0.5em;"} Recall that the "length" of an atomic vector describes the number of values in that vector and can be determined with `length()` (a primitive function): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length( c(0, 1, 1, 2) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 ``` ::: ::: The length of a list, however, is the number of list items -- it is *not* the number of values: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length( list( nerdy = "hello world", southern = "boy howdy", fibo_numbers = c(0, 1, 1, 2) ) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: The above list contains three list items (two one-value character vectors and a numeric vector with four values) -- thus `length()` returned the value `3`. *If the reason for this is not yet clear, content in **Lesson 1.5: Assignments** will help!* Because a data frame *is* a list, and each column represents a list item, the `length()` of a data frame is the number of columns: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} length(my_garden) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} True or false: For a data frame, `length()` returns the number of rows. ::: ### Heads and tails The dplyr package, part of the tidyverse core, contains a set of functions that start with the prefix `slice_` that allow you to print a subset of the data (see `?slice`). We can print the top row of a data frame using the function `slice_head()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} slice_head(my_garden) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost ``` ::: ::: ... or print the bottom row of a data frame using the function `slice_tail()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} slice_tail(my_garden) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-11-15 initial harvest ``` ::: ::: With the argument `n = [number of rows]`, we can subset to the number of rows of our choosing. For example, to subset the data to just the first two rows of the data frame, we can use: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} slice_head(my_garden, n = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} slice_tail(my_garden, n = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-11-02 shocked logs 2 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-11-15 initial harvest ``` ::: ::: ### Ordering Ordering a data frame is a great way to explore the values therein and look for potential problems. We can order an entire table by a variable's value using `arrange()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arrange(my_garden, bed) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 2 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 3 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 4 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs 5 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-08-21 shocked logs 6 0 deep shade shitake 2020-09-12 initial harvest 7 0 deep shade shitake 2020-10-08 shocked logs 8 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-10-17 initial harvest 9 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-11-02 shocked logs 10 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-11-15 initial harvest # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: This arranged the rows of the table by the values in the column `bed`. If we want to order the data frame from the largest to smallest values in a variable, we nest the function `desc()` inside of `arrange()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arrange( my_garden, desc(bed) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 2 6 full sun edamame 2020-04-15 planted 3 6 full sun corn 2020-04-21 planted 4 6 full sun acorn squash 2020-05-18 planted 5 6 full sun 2020-05-18 weeded 6 6 full sun 2020-05-18 weeded 7 6 full sun 2020-06-15 weeded 8 6 full sun 2020-06-15 weeded 9 6 full sun 2020-06-15 weeded 10 6 full sun corn 2020-07-28 eaten by bugs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: ### Characters & factors It is often necessary to know the unique values present in a set of characters or factors. We can subset a vector to its unique values using, appropriately, the function `unique()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} unique(my_garden$light_access) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "full sun" "deep shade" "shade" "partial shade" ``` ::: ::: *Note: The above works with any type of vector and the class of the output is equivalent to the original vector.* If the column is a factor, this information can also be extracted using the function `levels()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} levels( factor(my_garden$light_access) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "deep shade" "full sun" "partial shade" "shade" ``` ::: ::: If we want to see the number of records associated with a unique character or factor value, we can use the function `table()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} table(my_garden$light_access) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` deep shade full sun partial shade shade 10 27 5 3 ``` ::: ::: In the above, we are given a *very* handy printout of the distribution of the data! ### Statistical summaries When reading in data, it is often useful to look at the summary statistics for the dataset. This can help you find any errors (e.g., potential outliers or NA values). To do so, a good place to start is the function `summary()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(my_garden) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` bed light_access species date Min. :0.000 Length :45 Length :45 Min. :2019-10-28 1st Qu.:1.000 N.unique : 4 N.unique :11 1st Qu.:2020-04-12 Median :3.000 N.blank : 0 N.blank : 0 Median :2020-05-18 Mean :3.089 Min.nchar: 5 Min.nchar: 4 Mean :2020-05-16 3rd Qu.:6.000 Max.nchar:13 Max.nchar:16 3rd Qu.:2020-07-16 Max. :6.000 NAs :19 Max. :2020-11-15 event Length :45 N.unique :15 N.blank : 0 Min.nchar: 6 Max.nchar:26 ``` ::: ::: *Note: Notice that the printed summary information for character values is not particularly useful!* You can also look at summary statistics individually. This can be especially useful programmatically. I will not bore you with a lot of text to describe each one, but here are a few to try on your own (*see* `?[function_name]` *if you have any questions about what each does!*): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} min(my_garden$date) max(my_garden$date) mean(my_garden$date) median(my_garden$date) var(my_garden$date) sd(my_garden$date) ``` ::: ::: mysecret {{< fa user-secret size=2x >}}  [For God's sake, **do not** use `View()`!]{style="font-size: 20px"} There is one early exploration step that is commonly used that I *do not recommend* ... the function `View()`. This function allows you to view your data as though it were a spreadsheet. Here is how it is applied (I have not run it here, but you *may* run it on your own). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} View(my_garden) ``` ::: No matter how much I warn against this, you are going to use this function anyway, and when I see you do it during our help sessions, I will invariably complain -- I might even emit a high-pitched whiny squeal. The student response to my whining is usually something like "... but I like to see my data." You get very little information by looking directly at the data. There is no indication of column classes, no indication of the number of rows (without scrolling), it is nearly impossible to spot bad character or factor values, and there is little opportunity to explore numeric values (other than ordering). When the data get large, any utility of this tool quickly falls away. It is better to get in the practice of properly exploring the data. **Addendum**: I was recently working with a data frame that contained more than 20 columns. I ended up using `View()` because I needed to visually scan across many of those columns simultaneously. As such, it seems my warning above might be a little too absolute. ::: ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Check your understanding]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} Match each function to the information it provides.

::: ## Writing data Our final topic of this section is how to write data to a file. This is quite straightforward, so this section will (actually) be brief for once. To reduce clutter in your data folder, we will remove each file after writing. ### Atomic vectors There are two preferred ways to write an atomic vector to a file: as a *.txt* file or as an *.RDS* file. If you intend to share your vector outside of R, saving the vector as a text file is a great way to do it. To do so, use the `write_lines()` function. The first argument of the function is the data to write and the second argument is the relative file path: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_lines( unique(my_garden$light_access), file = "data/raw/temp.txt" ) ``` ::: We can use the `list.files()` function to see if the file was written: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} list.files("data/raw", pattern = "txt") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "temp.txt" ``` ::: ::: ... and *really* check to see if it worked by reading the data back in: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_lines("data/raw/temp.txt") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "full sun" "deep shade" "shade" "partial shade" ``` ::: ::: We will remove this file with `file.remove()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} file.remove("data/raw/temp.txt") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ... and check to see if we successfully removed the file: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} list.files("data/raw", pattern = "txt") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` character(0) ``` ::: ::: If you do not intend to use or share the data outside of R, your best bet is to save the data as an *.RDS* file. For this, we use the function `write_rds()`. Again, the first argument of the function is the data to write and the second argument is the relative file path: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Write light access to file: write_rds( factor(my_garden$light_access), file = "data/raw/temp.rds" ) # Did it work? read_rds("data/raw/temp.rds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] full sun full sun full sun full sun full sun [6] full sun deep shade deep shade deep shade deep shade [11] shade full sun full sun full sun partial shade [16] full sun full sun full sun full sun full sun [21] full sun full sun full sun shade shade [26] partial shade full sun full sun full sun partial shade [31] partial shade full sun full sun full sun full sun [36] partial shade full sun full sun deep shade deep shade [41] full sun deep shade deep shade deep shade deep shade Levels: deep shade full sun partial shade shade ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Yup, remove it! file.remove("data/raw/temp.rds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} list.files("data/raw", pattern = "rds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "angola_ungulates.rds" "coqui_counts.rds" "district_birds.rds" [4] "my_covid_garden.rds" ``` ::: ::: ::: mysecret    [When should I write a file as an RDS?]{style="font-size: 20px"} Reading and writing *.RDS* files is super straightforward in R. As stated previously, you maintain all of the attributes of the data and, frankly, little thought has to be given about the structure of the object. If you are happy with its current structure, you are good to go. That being said, **do not** write the file as an *.RDS* if: - You intend to share the file with a non-R-user - You plan to work with the file outside of R (hopefully, that will never be the case!) - The file is too big to fit in your memory **As a final note on RDS files**: While *.RDS* files are incredibly useful, I typically only write data as *.RDS* files during intermediate steps of a data management pipeline. Because they are platform-specific, and thus have limited portability across software and systems, they should not be used for long-term data storage. ::: ### Lists The **only** way that I save list-class objects is as an *.RDS* file! Let's make a list: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_list <- list( light_access = factor(my_garden$light_access), my_garden = my_garden ) ``` ::: ... save it as an *.RDS* file: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(my_list, file = "data/raw/temp.rds") ``` ::: ... check to see if it worked: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_rds("data/raw/temp.rds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $light_access [1] full sun full sun full sun full sun full sun [6] full sun deep shade deep shade deep shade deep shade [11] shade full sun full sun full sun partial shade [16] full sun full sun full sun full sun full sun [21] full sun full sun full sun shade shade [26] partial shade full sun full sun full sun partial shade [31] partial shade full sun full sun full sun full sun [36] partial shade full sun full sun deep shade deep shade [41] full sun deep shade deep shade deep shade deep shade Levels: deep shade full sun partial shade shade $my_garden # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: ... and remove the file: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} file.remove("data/raw/temp.rds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: I should note that you can use R to write a list as an Excel file (each list item is written to a separate worksheet). I do not recommend doing so, but the package `xlsx` has tools to accomplish this inadvisable task! ### Data frames The last kind of data we will write is a tibble. There are three options for doing so: - `write.csv()`: Base R version (**do not use!**) - `write_csv()`: readr version (use this!) - `write_rds()`: As above, handy if you do not intend to share the file with a non-R-user! Let's start with `write.csv()`. Again, we supply the dataset and a path to the file: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write.csv(my_garden, file = "data/raw/temp.csv") ``` ::: ... Let's see what the above returned: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_csv("data/raw/temp.csv") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 6 ...1 bed light_access species date event 1 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: We can see that this returned an additional column with (rarely useful) row numbers! Let's delete the file from our hard drive: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} file.remove("data/raw/temp.csv") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: mysecret    [Do not use `write.csv()`!]{style="font-size: 20px"} In these lessons we will *not* write files with `write.csv()`. Row numbers are rarely useful and, though you can supply an additional argument to avoid writing them, there is a better way ... ::: Use the *readr* function `write_csv()`! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_csv(my_garden, file = "data/raw/temp.csv") ``` ::: Let's see what the above returned: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} read_csv("data/raw/temp.csv") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ::: No row numbers! Let's delete the file: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} file.remove("data/raw/temp.csv") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: As above, we could have also written the file using `write_rds()` (but see caveats, above): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Write as an rds file: write_rds(my_garden, file = "data/raw/temp.rds") # Check to see if it worked: read_rds("data/raw/temp.rds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 45 × 5 bed light_access species date event 1 1 full sun 2019-10-28 applied compost 2 2 full sun 2019-10-29 applied compost 3 3 full sun 2019-11-01 applied compost 4 4 full sun 2019-11-05 applied compost 5 5 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 6 6 full sun 2019-11-08 applied compost 7 0 deep shade 2020-02-14 cut logs 8 0 deep shade lion's mane 2020-02-21 plugged logs 9 0 deep shade oyster mushrooms 2020-03-12 plugged logs 10 0 deep shade shitake 2020-03-15 plugged logs # ℹ 35 more rows ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Remove the file: file.remove("data/raw/temp.rds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: mysecret    [When should you write a file?]{style="font-size: 20px"} It is important to consider when a file should be written to your hard drive. Despite the number of files we will use in these lessons, I write files very rarely. Instead, once I get a raw data file, I generate a script for pre-processing the data and various wrangling steps. Rather than save the processed data, I save and run the script that executes the data processing. This helps ensure that I don't have multiple versions of the same data cluttering up my RStudio project folder. ::: ## Exercises ::: now_you {{< fa user-circle size=2x >}} [Test your knowledge!]{style="padding-left: 0.5em;"} 1. ::: ## Take-home points * Work inside an RStudio project and use paths that are relative to the project folder. * Choose an importing function that matches the file type. Read the messages printed during import and supply additional arguments when the file needs special handling. * Explore every data object after reading it. Check its structure, dimensions, ordering, unique values, and statistical summaries. * Choose an output format based on how the file will be used and who needs to open it. * Read important output files back into R. Confirm that the object was written as intended before continuing your analysis. ## Reference ::: panel - **csv file**: A file stored in the "comma separated values" format. This describes a plain text file where commas separate values and each record (e.g., row in a data frame) is placed on a new line. - **Project**: A collection of files that is referenced by a `.RProj` file. - **RDS file**: A storage format for data sets that are written in, and written for, program R. - **Relative file path**: The path to a file on your hard drive relative to the current working directory. ::: ::: panel **Important!** Primitive functions, as well as functions in the packages that R attaches by default (e.g., *base*, *utils*, *stats*, and *graphics*), are available as soon as you start an R session. ::: function_table ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
